extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of medieval Italian municipal history; scholars of Padua/Mantua governance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting descriptive rules, offices, eligibility, duties, and statutes governing Padua (and related notes on Mantua) in the medieval period as presented in a historical account. Focus is on institutional norms, procedural rules, and evaluative remarks about government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anciani membership requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: No man was admitted to this council of the anciani who was not a Padouan by birth, and an inhabitant of the city, for at least thirty years without interruption, and who had not a foundation of property among his fellow-citizens of at least two hundred pounds a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility is based on nativity, continuous residence (≥30 years), and a minimum property/income threshold (200 pounds/year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anciani duties (public utility & dispute conciliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To conciliate and appease all discords and dissensions among the citizens, not only in civil affairs but in criminal prosecutions; to see that the decrees of the senate regarding the public utility were observed; to propose to other councils things which might be of public utility; all public letters from foreign princes and from all magistrates within the dominion were read in their presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anciani acted as a standing body for conflict resolution, oversight of public works/utilities, and as a forum for receiving official communications. They functioned as an advisory and supervisory council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lesser Council composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lesser Council at first consisted of forty citizens, partly noble and partly plebeian, afterwards increased to the number of sixty. Nothing could be treated in the greater council if it were not first discussed and agitated here, and from hence proposed to the greater council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Served as preliminary deliberative body; membership mixed nobility/plebeians; increase in size over time; acted as a gatekeeper for items reaching the greater council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation procedure and voting threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of discussing and consulting upon business was by way of orations or harangues made by the senators, after which they proceeded to a vote, and two thirds of the suffrages determined the question. This rule was also observed in the greater council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal deliberation via speeches followed by a supermajority (2/3) decision rule in both lesser and greater councils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lesser Council rotation and exclusion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: This council was changed every four months, and the senators who had once been in it must be excluded for eight months. Father and son, brothers, and uncle and nephew, were not permitted to sit together in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent rotation and cooling-off period to prevent entrenchment; explicit prohibition on close relatives serving simultaneously to limit nepotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lesser Council eligibility (additional conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be of this council it was necessary to be a Padouan by origin, to have a father who was a Padouan by birth, to have inhabited in Padoua with a family at least for forty years continually, to have an estate of fifty pounds income, and to have submitted to the offices of the commons of the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stricter nativity and residence rules than anciani (father native, 40 years continuous residence), lower property threshold (50 pounds) and prior civic service required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater Council (Parliament) composition and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greater Council, or Parliament: it was at first of three hundred senators (one moiety nobles and the other moiety plebeians); it was afterwards increased to six hundred, and finally, in 1277, to a thousand, in which were chosen the magistrates, and all affairs relative to peace and war were deliberated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large mixed assembly responsible for selecting magistrates and deciding major matters of state (peace and war); membership size evolved over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custody of municipal law copies
rubrics_metrics.description: By a determination of 1263, various municipal laws and statutes were made four copies. The first was deposited in the monastery of St. Benedict, the second in that of St. John, the third in that of St. Mary, and the fourth in that of the fathers of St. Mary di Porciglia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decentralized archival practice: four canonical repositories for municipal laws to ensure preservation and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta: purpose and desired qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Padouans, desirous of providing a remedy against the disorders and mischiefs occasioned by the consulate, invented the annual magistrate of the podesta, ... a foreign personage, of noble blood, and excellent reputation for virtue, who, by the weight and eminence of his authority ... was called by way of eminence the Podesta.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Podesta intended as an external, neutral executive with moral authority to mediate factional conflict; selection favored foreign nobility reputed for virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta pre-election/selection procedure (sequestered ballot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three months before the end of his government ... to be elected eight citizens, four noble and four plebeian, ... these elected twelve senators ... who ... elected eight others ... These were shut up together in one apartment, and could not speak to any one, or have more than one repast a day, that they might the sooner agree in the nomination of three personages, who were afterwards carried to the greater council, who proceeded to the election in this manner: All three were separately ballotted for, and he who had the most suffrages was the new podesta; he who had the next number of votes held the second place; and he who had fewest the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-stage, confined, secretive selection process intended to limit outside influence and expedite consensus; final choice made by ballot among three nominees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta acceptance and record of refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: The syndick of the city was sent in haste with public letters to him who had been honoured with most votes, who, if he accepted the charge, was understood to be podesta; but if in four days he did not accept it, the syndick was sent to the second; and if he refused, the third was sent to; and if he declined, a new election was made of other three persons; and of the acceptance or refusal of these a record was made by a notary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal notification and limited acceptance window (four days) with documented acceptance/refusal to ensure accountability in selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta statutory ineligibility (consanguinity/banishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: No man could be elected podesta who had in Padoua relations, by consanguinity or affinity, within the fourth degree, nor who had been banished from his country for forgery or treason; and this was also understood of the court or retinue which the podesta brought with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions designed to prevent local familial influence and to exclude individuals with prior serious criminal banishments; applies to principal and his immediate retinue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta household and retinue restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The podesta, judges, and lieutenants, could not have with them in Padoua their wives, nor other ladies their relations, unless for fifteen days, on occasion of infirmity, nor even their brothers, sons, or nephews, more than twelve years of age, nor servants who should be Padouans. The podesta was obliged to bring with him his two lieutenants, twelve iatcihites, twelve horses, twelve valets and servants, and all this family and these horses to be maintained at his expense, for the public service of the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits domestic entourage to reduce local influence and nepotism; certain specified retinue components required and maintained at the podesta's expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta salary and term timing
rubrics_metrics.description: His salary was two thousand five hundred pounds a year, and was afterwards increased to four thousand. The podestarate began on the first of July; but in 1280 it was decreed to begin the first of January. This magistracy at first continued for a year; but in 1294 a law was made that it should endure only six months, and that two podestas should be created each year, one to begin his administration with January, the other with July.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation and term length evolved: initial annual term and mid-year start later changed to fixed January/July starts and ultimately to two six-month terms per year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta oath of office
rubrics_metrics.description: He was obliged to take the oath of office, viz. to swear that he, with his judges, would govern without ambition, and justly, and that they would give the greatest attention to the affairs of the public, and with all their power would conciliate and pacify the controversies and discords of the citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal commitment to impartiality, justice, public service, and conflict resolution required before assuming office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta immediate obligations (three days: papal constitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: First: in the space of three days, to cause to be read, and afterwards to cause to be punctually observed, the papal constitutions against heretics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early, public enforcement of papal decrees as a condition of authority—indicates religious-legal obligations tied to civic governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta residence and judicial openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, to reside continually in the city, and rule it until the arrival of a successor. Thirdly, during the whole time of his administration, to hear the causes of all persons indifferently, to which end the gates of the palace, except at the hour of dinner, should always stand open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation of continuous presence and accessible justice—open court access as an anti-privilege measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta role in ecclesiastical appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourthly, that, together with the anciani, he should use all his endeavours that the canonicates, and the other ecclesiastical benefices, of the bishopric and diocese of Padoua, should be conferred on citizens of Padoua, or of her district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic influence over local ecclesiastical benefices to favor local citizens/district—blending civic and ecclesiastical patronage responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta duties for city defence and militia
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifthly, to elect eight citizens, men of prudence and experience, two for each quarter, who should make choice of four or five hundred able men, who, when they should hear the sound of the palace bells, should come armed, under their standards, to the palace of the pretor, and to the piazza del Vino, for its defence. Sixthly, to give orders that, at the sound of the great bell of the tower of the palace, all the citizens and inhabitants of Padoua, from sixteen to sixty years of age, should run armed to the piazza to defend the common liberty. Seventhly, to create a captain, who, with some soldiers, should have the custody of the city and its suburbs. Eighthly, to hold, night and day, guards at the gates of the city. Ninthly, to give orders that in the city and in the suburbs should be kept cross-bows, and other weapons, to exercise the soldiers. Tenthly, to cause to be enrolled in the militia many men of the villages, who, according to occurrences, should come armed to the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive defence responsibilities: raising, organizing, and training militia; maintaining arms and permanent guards; mobilization procedures on sound of bells; creation of military captain and garrison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta crowd control and standard-bearing assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Eleventhly, in all great tumult to order into the piazza the standards of the community; in which case standard-bearers of the arts, at the sound of the bells of the palace, were held to go to the piazza del Vino, with the men under their command, armed, ready to obey whatever orders the podesta should issue, and there assemble, to be formed into a body, under the ensigns of the community, which could not depart from the piazza without the express command of the podesta himself, for whose guard there were always five hundred soldiers elected, one hundred from the body of the patricians, and four hundred from the plebeians, distinguished into four squadrons, under four standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalized civic militia structure with guild/arts standard-bearers, centralized command by podesta, and explicit limits on deployment (cannot depart without podesta order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Podesta restrictions on sentencing near end of term
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelfthly, that for eight days before the arrival of a successor, the podesta cannot give sentence in civil or criminal causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitation to prevent last-minute abuses of power and protect due process as term ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-term accountability (fourteen-day complaints procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirteenthly, that having finished his podestarate, he, his assessors, and courtiers, should remain fourteen days in Padoua, to render an account before the syndick of their administration, which is done in this manner: For the three first days it was lawful to every one to accuse the podesta, assessors, and courtiers, before the syndicks, of any wrongs or injuries done them: in the eight following days these complaints were determined by the votes of the major part of the syndicks; and if, by the multitude of complaints, or by differences of opinions among the syndicks, or through other reasons, the business could not be finished, three other days were added, in which the syndicks were obliged to determine it. From the defence against the complaints made against the podesta were excluded all his favourites, friends, and relations, and all advocates; his own judges and assessors were alone admitted, and were thought sufficient for his defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured, time-limited public accountability with restricted defence privileges; designed to enable citizen complaints and syndick adjudication soon after term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-term disqualification from office
rubrics_metrics.description: He could not be confirmed in the podestarate for the next year, nor for the five following years; neither himself, nor any of his relations, could hold any office, dignity, or honours, in the city of Padoua; and this was understood of the assessors, lieutenants of police, and other officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooling-off and anti-entrenchment rule preventing immediate reappointment or familial accession to office to limit consolidation of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' roles and rotation to prevent corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of the first judge was to assist the podesta in all things belonging to the government of the city; the other three judges had the charge of hearing and trying the criminal causes, each one for three months, which was ordained to remove all occasion of full suspicion that the accused by length of time might possibly corrupt the judges: but these orders were afterwards changed, and it was resolved that the first judge, who must be an eminent doctor of laws, should be the vicar of the podesta, that the second should judge criminal causes, the third should have the charge of the provisions, and that the fourth should be questor and receiver of the public money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial duties initially rotated frequently (3-month criminal terms) to limit corruption; later specialized roles assigned including a legal vicar, criminal judge, provisioning officer, and financial receiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower courts and arbitration for family disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain other judges were instituted, called Judges of the Lower Courts, and were distinguished from each other by the names of animals... For the suits arising between relations, two judges were instituted as arbitrators, who, in the space of two months, were to give sentence, and terminate the controversy: and if they could not agree, they called in ten jurors for each party; and if these disagreed, the podesta himself, in the space of fifteen days, sat in judgment with the rest, and decided the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tiered dispute resolution: lower courts, time-limited arbitration for kin disputes, escalation to jurors, then to podesta if unresolved—formalized deadlines to ensure resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute abolishing private jurisdiction of life and death (1200/1205)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the year 1200, a law was made, that, under pain of death, no man should, for the future, exercise any jurisdiction in the territory of Padoua; this law was re-enacted and confirmed in 1205. The jurisdiction of life and death, and all other jurisdiction, being taken away from these grandees, the whole territory was governed by the podesta of Padoua.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abolished feudal/lordly capital jurisdiction to centralize justice in civic magistracy; enforced under severe penalty to curb local lordly cruelty/abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on podestas in outlying districts (statute 1290)
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom of sending podestas into the districts continued till 1290, when a statute was made, that places which were not walled should not have a podesta, but that into some of them vicars only should be sent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiated governance for rural/unwalled places by substituting vicars for podestas—recognition of administrative/defence limits of smaller localities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunes (gastaldi) institution and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The plebeians demanded and obtained the institution of a magistrate, like a tribune of the people (the Padouans called these magistrates Gastaldi dell'Arti), who should defend the rights of the plebeians, and have authority to rescind all those determinations of the senate ... In 1296 a statute that on the first Sunday in every month the gastaldi should all assemble in the church of the palace of the commons, and treat fully of all things that belonged to the state of the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunes/gastaldi had veto/rescission powers over senate acts, regular monthly assembly, and represented guild/plebeian interests—an institutional check that could become powerful and abusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of tribunate ascendancy and factional abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole government of the city, by this alteration, devolved into the hands of the tribunes, because they annulled or confirmed at their pleasure the determinations of the greater council ... From this disorderly and violent domination of the tribunes ... grew intestine hatreds and terrible seditions ... the tribunship of the people was abolished in the year 1314, and the government and the public authority was transferred to the patricians, excluding totally the plebeians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical anti-pattern: the institutional empowerment of tribunes led to factional capture, enrichment, violent conflict, and eventual suppression—illustrates risks of unchecked popular magistracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative principle: need for distinct executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: The great desideratum in a government is a distinct executive power, of sufficient strength and weight to compel both these parties, in turn, to submit to the laws. The absence of a third power to mediate between them prevented balance and produced instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial evaluative criterion: effective governance requires a neutral, sufficiently strong executive and some mediating power between factions to secure stability and protect life, liberty, and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of mixed assemblies without mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: At times the sovereignty was clearly in one assembly of optimates or patricians; at another in one assembly of plebeians... there being no third power to mediate between them, no balance could be formed or maintained between them. The consequence was instability to the laws, insecurity to life, liberty, and property, constant rivalry between the principal families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational criterion linking institutional structure (absence of balancing power) to negative outcomes; useful as evaluative standard when assessing other municipal constitutions.
